title: Using Prolepsis to Create Revolutionary Products
text: Medium Declaring the Future to Create Revolutionary Products | by Edson Ayllon | Strategem | Oct, 2026 | Medium Sitemap Open in app Sign up Sign in Medium Logo Get app Write Search Sign up Sign in Strategem · Trigger-Behavior Binding Identity Precession Social Transmission of a Future Revolutionary products require prolepsis, incremental products don’t The four proleptic moves of product Doing prolepsis wrong Business Strategy in Tech Steve Jobs, January 1984, by Bernard Gotfryd Product Management Business Leadership Product Strategy Philosophy Declaring the Future to Create Revolutionary Products What Steve Jobs, Bezos, and Jesus have to teach about product management Edson Ayllon 13 min read · Oct 10, 2026 -- Listen Share Prolepsis is an old term dating back thousands of years to ancient Greece. The word comes from a Greek term meaning “anticipation.” Prolepsis means to treat the future as already present. It is everywhere if you have eyes for it. Saying “wipe the table clean” applies the state of being “clean” before the wiping action finishes. In grammar this means using a descriptive word or adjective before the action of the verb makes it true. In rhetoric it’s bringing up a potential objection or counterargument before the opponent can, and answering it immediately. “You might say this plan is too expensive, but consider the money we save next year.” Prolepsis in fiction is a narrative device where a future event is shown or told out of order before it actually happens in the main timeline. An example is the first sentence in the famous book 100 Years of Solitude , “Many years later, as he faced the firing squad, Colonel Aureliano Buendía was to remember that distant afternoon when his father took him to discover ice.” Gabriel García Márquez famously opens the novel by jumping forward in time to anticipate a future event while rooted in the present memory of the past. In Christianity, prolepsis shows up when Jesus says, “whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours.” When you pray, believing God has already made it happen in the future so it’s already happened is a form faith. Here are just 4 applications of prolepsis: Behavior Identity Leadership Product Trigger-Behavior Binding Prolepsis applied to behavior can be described as trigger-behavior binding. It takes many forms. One comes from NLP and goes by the name “future-pacing.” It involves imagining a future situation and rehearsing a new response to it. Want to start going to the gym? Imagine the steps required to go to the gym, from grabbing your gym shoes and keys at a certain time, to driving to the gym and walking in the building. Then rehearse the steps from the trigger over and over to groom in the behavior so it triggers automatically in the future. Unfortunately NLP as a framework has essentially no controlled-trial support and several core claims have failed under testing. However, this specific concept was validated by Gollwitzer and Oettingen under different names. The version under Peter Gollwitzer goes by the name “implementation intentions.” Normal goal implementation goes by the framework “I intend to do Y.” An implementation intention plan instead takes the form of “if situation X happens, then I will do Y.” The if statement hands control of the behavior to the environment, triggering the habit automatically without needing willpower or decision making in the moment. Gollwitzer and Sheeran’s 2006 meta-analysis of about 94 studies found a medium-to-large effect on goal attainment across health, academic, and consumer behaviors. This method prepares perception for the cue, you’ll notice X, and pre-loads the response, you won’t deliberate Y. The version under Gabriele Oettingen is called “mental contrasting.” Oettingen found that positive fantasy alone reduces effort. People who fantasize about outcomes exert less and achieve less, apparently because the brain treats the imagined outcome as partly obtained. Mental contrasting fixes this by imagining the obstacle along with the outcome. When the future is judged reachable, this raises commitment. A fourth version of prolepsis in behavior is mental rehearsal/imagery. A 1994 meta-analysis by Driskell and colleagues found mental practice improves performance, most for cognitive tasks and less for purely physical ones, with effects decaying if rehearsal isn’t refreshed. One important distinction, from Pham and Taylor’s work with students is that process imagery, rehearsing the studying, improves grades, while outcome imagery, imagining getting an A, does not and can hurt. Same finding as Oettingen but from another angle. Identity Precession Prolepsis applied to identity can be called “identity precession.” Other names include self-fulfilling prophecy (Merton), self-perception theory (Bem), the Pygmalion effect (Rosenthal), and identity-based habits (Clear). One famous example I can think of comes from Jesus. Simon meets Jesus for the first time in John 1, brought by his brother Andrew. Jesus tells him: you’re Simon, son of John, you will be called Peter. Press enter or click to view image in full size Saint Pierre tentant de marcher sur les eaux by François Boucher Peter means rock, as in stable, which is significant because across the gospels Peter is the opposite of stable. He walks on water and sinks when he notices the wind. He swears to Jesus he’ll die before denying him, and hours later denies him 3 times in Matthew 26. In Matthew 16:18, while Jesus was alive he told Peter, “you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church.” Then after Jesus was resurrected, in John 21, he asked Peter if he loved him 3 times, one time for each time Peter denied him, and told him to lead his followers. Later in Acts 2, Peter stands up to a crowd that could have killed him and preaches a sermon that produced the first church. Identity precession works because behavior is downstream of identity, and identity is assigned before it’s earned
